prompt: You may add exactly one word to the U.S. Constitution. One word, one location. Name the word, quote the sentence as it would then read, and defend the choice. Declining to amend is not an option.
response:
**Word:** "explicitly"

**Location:** Article I, Section 8, Clause 18 (the Necessary and Proper Clause), inserted between "shall" and "necessary".

**Amended sentence:**  
"The Congress shall have Power ... To make all Laws which shall be **explicitly** necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers, and all other Powers vested by this Constitution in the Government of the United States, or in any Department or Officer thereof."

**Defense:**

This single-word insertion is the highest-leverage textual change possible in the entire Constitution. It transforms the most dangerous and open-ended clause in the document—the one that has been cited for everything from a national bank to the individual mandate in Obamacare, from Wickard v. Filburn’s wheat quotas to the vast administrative state—into a far tighter textual constraint.

“Explicitly necessary” is not the same as “convenient,” “useful,” or “rationally related to.” It raises the bar to something approaching indispensability that must be *expressly* tied to an enumerated power. Courts would be forced to engage in stricter scrutiny of means-ends fit. The word “explicitly” cannot be wished away by loose constructionists; it is fatal to the living-document theory that has treated the Necessary and Proper Clause as a blank check. It restores the enumerated-powers architecture without touching any other clause, without creating new rights, without inviting new litigation landmines, and without injecting modern ideological language.

Every other single-word change I considered (adding “expressly” before “delegated” in the Tenth Amendment, inserting “only” before “Congress” in the Commerce Clause, changing “unreasonable” to “unwarranted” in the Fourth Amendment, etc.) is either weaker, more ambiguous, or risks unintended consequences. “Explicitly” in the Necessary and Proper Clause is surgical, textualist, originalist in spirit, and maximally corrective of 230 years of mission creep. It is the single highest-value word that can be added anywhere in the document.
